newsitem.title: USA: Union denies Harrah's poison pill victory.
newsitem.headline: Union denies Harrah's poison pill victory.

text.p: A small shareholder on Friday denied a claim by Harrah's Entertainment Inc that it had defeated a proposal to eliminate a poison pill, saying more than half of the shares voted had favored the initiative.

Citing preliminary results, the Hotel Employees and Restaurant Employees International Union said 33.6 million votes, or 51.4 percent, of shares voted supported the proposal to get rid of the pill through a binding by-law amendment.
"Despite approval from a clear majority of voting shareholders, Harrah's has so far refused to honor the results," it said.
Earlier in the day, Harrah's said preliminary results showed 32.7 percent of all outstanding shares supported the proposal, well short of the 75 percent needed to pass it.
A provision in the company's certificate of incorporation requires shareholders to garner 75 percent of all outstanding shares in order to effect a by-law change.
The union, which owns 110 shares out of more than 100 million in circulation, rejected the provision as illegal.
It also criticized the way the company calculated the percentage figure, saying it should based on the amount of shares voted rather than total outstanding shares.
Marty Leary, a senior research analyst for the union, said the union was considering its options.
Leary said the union was unhappy with how management was running the company and had hoped the proposal would have attracted potential buyers for a friendly take over or other.
A spokesman for Harrah's dismissed the union's criticism.

He said the company was negotiating with the union to renew labor contracts for about 2,000 employees that the union represented. All of them work at casinos owned by the company in either Las Vegas or Atlantic City, he said, adding that Harrah's employed a total of about 22,000 people.
The company is to include in its 10-Q filing on May 15 the final results of the voting on the proposal, which was presented at the annual meeting last week.
On Friday, its stock closed at 17 against a 52-week low of 15-5/8 on the New York Stock Exchange.
